demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is 35, married, and works as a counselor, a role that has long depended on her ability to stay steady in the face of other people’s pain. Before the accident, she describes herself as someone who could listen without flinching, someone friends and clients alike turned to when things felt unmanageable. That sense of herself changes in a single afternoon, when a routine driving mistake becomes the moment around which her life begins to organize.

She is driving in familiar conditions, on a road she has taken many times, when everything happens too quickly for her mind to make sense of it in the moment. She misjudges, something goes wrong, and another person is seriously injured. She does not talk about the details of the impact first; she talks about the sound. The sound is what stays with her. In the immediate aftermath, she moves as if through water, stunned and mechanically focused on what must be done next. She remembers getting out of the car, remembers panic rising in her throat, remembers the sickening realization that someone else is hurt because of her. Even now, she returns to the same sequence over and over, as if replaying it might produce a different ending.

In the days that follow, she cannot stop seeing the injured person’s body in her mind. Images interrupt her at work, in the shower, while standing at the kitchen counter, while trying to fall asleep beside her husband. She begins to avoid driving whenever possible and arranges her life so that other people will take the wheel. When she cannot avoid it, she grips the seatbelt tightly and scans the road with an intensity that leaves her exhausted before she arrives. She no longer trusts ordinary moments. A green light, a sudden brake, the squeal of tires in a parking lot can make her heart slam against her ribs. She startles more easily than she used to and feels embarrassed by how quickly her body reacts, as if it is preparing for catastrophe before her mind can catch up.

As a counselor, she is used to sitting with distress, but after the accident her work becomes complicated in ways she did not expect. She continues seeing clients, yet she notices herself becoming overly alert to any mention of injury, guilt, or responsibility. A story about an accident can make her lose her thread. Sometimes she feels a wave of nausea in the middle of a session and has to focus on breathing while still appearing present and calm. She worries constantly that she will say the wrong thing, that she will somehow betray her own role by being less composed than the people sitting across from her. At times, she feels ashamed for finding other people’s trauma easier to hold than her own. The shame sharpens her silence. She does not tell colleagues much, and at home she gives short answers, trying to protect her husband from the parts of her that feel damaged and frighteningly changeable.

At night, sleep does not come easily. If she does sleep, she wakes suddenly from dreams that leave her disoriented and sweating, with her body already braced for danger. She begins checking and rechecking things: the lock on the door, the stove, the route she will take the next morning. She knows the checking does not bring real relief, but she cannot seem to stop. Her thoughts circle the same questions: Why did I not see it sooner? Why did I not do something differently? She returns to the belief that one decision, one second, one lapse defines her more fully than anything else in her life.

Her marriage becomes quieter during this time. Her husband wants to help, and she can see that he is careful with her, but she often feels separate from him, as though she is living behind glass. Some days she wants comfort and cannot reach for it. Other days she is irritated by his concern and then immediately ashamed of the irritation. She misses her old ease, her old confidence in competence and care. She still functions, still works, still attends to obligations, but there is a constant undercurrent of dread and self-reproach that colors nearly everything she does. Even moments of calm feel fragile, as if one small cue could bring the whole event rushing back.

Now, months later, she is still trying to make sense of the fact that she is both the one who caused harm and the one who cannot stop suffering from it. She does not describe herself as fearless anymore. She describes herself as careful, watchful, and tired. The accident remains with her not only as a memory, but as a presence that changes how she drives, how she listens, how she sleeps, and how she experiences her own mind.
